newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Le Pen not invited to Pope rally - church.
newsitem.headline: France's Le Pen not invited to Pope rally - church.

text.p: Church authorities denied on Monday that far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen had been invited to attend a mass celebrated by Pope John Paul during a forthcoming visit to France.

Le Pen had said that European Parliament members had been invited to the Pope's celebration of the 1,500th anniversary of the baptism of pagan king Clovis in Reims on Sunday, and that he would attend in that capacity.

"Some people think the country, the nation, history, all that is not important, that we are French because we live here or because we just happened to be born here," Le Pen, under fire for saying races are unequal, told France-3 television in a Sunday evening interview.

"I believe in the past, I believe in roots, I am proud of belonging to an ancient country...I will therefore be where the Pope will be, among the deputies because I am a European (Parliament) deputy," he said.
But Father Bernard Goureau, spokesman for the Reims archbishop, said Le Pen was not on the list of 393 guests invited by the archbishop of the northeastern city.
"As far as the archbishop and organisers are aware, the European deputies never made themselves heard and there is no group of European deputies," he said.
Church officials said Le Pen was free to attend the Papal rally as a private citizen but that he would not be able to sit in the area reserved for guests.
"He hasn't been invited. He won't be turned away if he turns up, but he won't be given a seat," said a spokesman for the bishops' conference in Paris.
Le Pen had said that he would go to Reims to honour the head of the Roman Catholic Church, who will visit France for four days from Thursday, and to honour 1,500 years of French history.
There was no immediate comment from Le Pen's National Front party.

Clovis, a pagan king who was the first west European monarch to convert to Roman Catholicism, has been hijacked as a symbol of the National Front. It says white, Christian French civilisation is superior to others.

Mainstream politicians have savaged Le Pen for saying racial differences are "a fact". But almost all shied away from proposals to ban his party, fearing a backlash of sympathy for his anti-immigrant views.
